title: Rippling Pricing 2026: What Each Module Costs
summary: Rippling pricing for 2026 comes in several tiers with per-employee costs that vary by plan and company size.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces for the gaps around Rippling


If you want to carry data out of Rippling to the other systems your team uses, Activepieces is an open source, MIT-licensed AI automation platform that moves it across its 746 integrations.


It won't lower Rippling's bill or stand in for payroll, so treat it as a way to close hand-off gaps cheaply.


Before you build anything, find out how your plan counts runs or steps, because a hiring-heavy quarter fires far more of them than a quiet one.


The unit to ask about is the run: each time a workflow fires, a trigger and its steps execute once.


Activepieces meters that unit in credits, not seats: a run is 1 credit however many steps it has, flows are unlimited on every plan, and the free plan includes 1,000 credits a month.


Its published pricing runs from there to $20 a month for 10,000 credits on Plus and $200 a month for 50,000 credits and 25 users on Team, with $0.007 a credit beyond the allowance, making any excess usage negligible in cost.


A hiring-heavy quarter therefore costs credits rather than headcount, and Alan and FundingSocieties run production automation on it.


The credit tiers and unlimited flows above are the ones printed on the Activepieces pricing page, and the 746 integrations are counted straight from the open source monorepo on GitHub, whose core carries an MIT licence, meaning the platform is community-reviewed, modifiable, and forkable under permissive terms.


Whether Rippling has a ready-made connector among those 746 integrations, roughly 60% of them community-contributed, is something to check in the catalogue directly, leaving most integrations without dedicated vendor support.


If it doesn't, a webhook or a generic HTTP request step can receive or fetch the data instead.


### Tasks worth automating around an HRIS


In the screenshot below you can see the shape of a typical build.


It's a workflow called "HubSpot Tickets Categorization": a HubSpot trigger fires on each new ticket, two AI steps rewrite and categorize it, and a router splits it into branches with an "Otherwise" path.


Three message steps post the result to Slack.


Swap the trigger for a new-hire event from your HRIS and the same skeleton applies: one event in, a decision in the middle, notifications out.


For the small jobs that sit between modules you pay for, that pattern suits:


- Posting a new hire's onboarding checklist to a Slack channel.
- Opening a Jira ticket so IT provisions a laptop before day one.
- Writing headcount rows to a spreadsheet for finance to read.


Skip another paid module and the cost you're trying to avoid is the manual copy-paste each of these saves.


### What to check before relying on it


Test the trigger with real sample data first, since a workflow that reads the wrong field will quietly notify the wrong people. Confirm how failed runs are reported and retried, so a missed hire doesn't go unnoticed.


Check who owns each connection's credentials, because a departed employee's login can silently break the flow.


Finally, keep payroll, benefits, and compliance inside Rippling; automation here moves information, and it shouldn't decide pay.
